subject: Economy
theme: Sectoral composition and GDP contribution ranking in the Indian economy
question_short_text: Decreasing order of GDP contribution by four specified sectors at 2000-01 constant prices
text:
Which of the following represents the decreasing order of the contribution of these sectors to the Gross Domestic Product (GDP) at factor cost at constant prices (2000-01)?

1. Agriculture, Forestry and Fishing
2. Manufacturing
3. Trade, Hotels Transport and Communication
4. Financing, Insurance, Real Estate and Business services
explanation: The correct decreasing order of GDP contribution at 2000-01 constant prices is: Trade, Hotels Transport and Communication (3), followed by Financing, Insurance, Real Estate and Business Services (4), then Agriculture, Forestry and Fishing (1), and finally Manufacturing (2). This reflects India's transition toward a services-dominated economy.

research.summary: This 2002 question tests a fundamental concept in the UPSC syllabus: understanding India's structural economic shift from agriculture to services. At the turn of the millennium (2000-01 constant prices baseline), the ranking 3-4-1-2 reveals an important economic reality that distinguishes UPSC questions from naive expectations. The trap is that many students assume agriculture or manufacturing would be the top contributors because they seem 'fundamental' to a developing economy. However, by 2000, India had already undergone decades of service-sector growth driven by IT, finance, and telecommunications liberalization post-1991. Sector 3 (Trade, Hotels, Transport, Communication) is broader and includes retail commerce, which has high employment and value addition. Sector 4 (Financing, Insurance, Real Estate, Business Services) had surged due to banking sector growth, the emergence of private insurance, and real estate expansion in post-1991 India. Agriculture (1), despite employing a large workforce, contributes relatively less to GDP because of lower per-unit productivity. Manufacturing (2), while important, was still not as significant as services by 2000-01. The key insight is that at constant prices (adjusting for inflation), nominal values collapse to real growth rates, and services had outpaced manufacturing growth in the 1990s. This question rewards students who understand the broad shift in India's economy since independence—from 55% primary sector in 1950-51 to less than 25% by 2000, with services rising from under 30% to nearly 50% by that time. A student who memorizes the current sector shares (2024-25: services ~55%, industry ~27%, agriculture ~17%) without understanding the historical trend will miss this one.
facts: In 1950-51, the primary sector (agriculture) contributed over 55% of India's GDP, while services contributed only around 28%; by 2000-01, this had reversed dramatically with services near 50% and primary sector around 20-22%.

The 1991 economic liberalization unlocked rapid growth in financial services, IT, telecommunications, and real estate, transforming the services sector into India's GDP growth engine well before 2000-01.

Manufacturing in India grew but remained constrained by industrial licensing (abolished only in 1991) and infrastructure bottlenecks, resulting in slower expansion compared to trade and services in the 1990s.

The services sector's definition in Indian national accounts includes retail trade, hospitality, transport, and communication—all of which grew significantly post-1991 due to urbanization and consumer demand.

At constant prices (2000-01), nominal inflation is stripped out, so the ranking reflects real sectoral growth rates; services had achieved higher real growth momentum by 2000 than manufacturing or agriculture.
